title: Seven Historic Indian Palaces and Forts Now Serving Fine Cuisine
excerpt: From Jodhpur's sandstone havelis to Mumbai's converted ice factories, India's architectural landmarks are finding new life as dining destinations that pair heritage preservation with regional gastronomy.
body:
• Centuries-old palaces, forts and colonial-era structures across India are being restored and converted into fine-dining restaurants, preserving architectural heritage through adaptive reuse.
  • Standout venues include Darikhana in an 18th-century Jodhpur haveli, Adaa inside Hyderabad's 1884 Falaknuma Palace, and 1135 AD within the UNESCO-listed Amer Fort.
  • The trend extends beyond Rajasthan, with projects like Native Bombay transforming a 19th-century ice factory and Lakhori reviving a Mughal-era haveli in Old Delhi.
  • Heritage dining appeals strongly to the Indian diaspora as a way to reconnect with cultural roots through immersive culinary experiences during visits home.

Dining Inside History

India's centuries-old palaces and forts are no longer confined to museum tours and photo ops. A growing number of heritage structures—sandstone havelis, Mughal mansions, Nizam-era palaces, colonial-era factories—have been carefully restored and reopened as restaurants, according to a roundup by The Indian Express. The conversions preserve original architectural elements while adapting the spaces for modern diners, creating what conservationists describe as one of the more effective models of adaptive reuse in the country.

The trend spans at least seven major heritage dining destinations across six cities, each offering a distinct slice of India's architectural past alongside regional cuisine.

Rajasthan Leads the Way

Rajasthan, with its dense concentration of palaces and forts, dominates the heritage dining scene. In Jodhpur, Darikhana occupies an 18th-century sandstone haveli within the RAAS Haveli complex, overlooking Mehrangarh Fort. The restaurant's colonnaded verandahs and stone jaalis have been preserved intact, with minimalist contemporary interiors layered over the original structure.

Jaipur alone claims three heritage restaurants. Baradari, located within the City Palace complex, transforms a 14,000-square-foot royal courtyard into a fine-dining space featuring translucent marble, mirrorwork and water cascades. The restaurant is widely regarded as one of India's finest examples of heritage-led hospitality.

"The result is an immersive experience where the setting is every bit as memorable as the cuisine."

— The Indian Express

Also in Jaipur, 1135 AD sits within the royal quarters of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed Amer Fort, where diners eat beneath ornate frescoes, sandstone arches and Sheesh Mahal mirror inlays. In Udaipur, Palki Khana—once used to store royal palanquins—has been converted into a restaurant inside the City Palace, retaining its original carved pillars, marble flooring and Rajasthani craftsmanship.

Beyond Rajasthan: Hyderabad, Delhi and Mumbai

The heritage dining movement extends well beyond Rajasthan's palace circuit. In Hyderabad, Adaa operates inside the Taj Falaknuma Palace, a 19th-century structure built between 1884 and 1893 by Nawab Vikar-ul-Umra. The palace's Italian marble floors, carved walnut ceilings and 40 Venetian chandeliers have been meticulously preserved, with the restaurant serving traditional Hyderabadi cuisine in what was once the Nizam's private quarters.

In Old Delhi, Lakhori occupies Haveli Dharampura, a 19th-century Mughal mansion dating to 1887 that underwent years of painstaking conservation. The restoration preserved original courtyards, carved jharokhas, lime-plastered walls and the traditional lakhori bricks that give the restaurant its name. The haveli sits in the narrow lanes of Shahjahanabad, serving North Indian cuisine in a setting that recalls the old city's Mughal-era grandeur.

Mumbai contributes Native Bombay, housed inside the restored Ambico Ice Factory in Ballard Estate—a late 19th-century industrial structure. Rather than erasing the building's industrial past, architects retained exposed brick walls, teak trusses, towering ceilings and vintage machinery, creating an unusual fusion of heritage preservation and contemporary design.

A Preservation Model That Works

The restaurant conversion model has drawn attention from conservationists because it provides a sustainable economic rationale for heritage preservation. Unlike museums, which depend on government funding and visitor fees, heritage restaurants generate ongoing commercial revenue that funds continued maintenance and restoration.

The approach also makes heritage accessible in ways that traditional preservation cannot. Diners spend hours inside these structures, engaging with architectural details—carved stonework, hand-painted frescoes, original brass fittings—that might receive only a passing glance during a guided tour.

Why It Matters for the Diaspora

For members of the Indian diaspora planning visits home, heritage restaurants offer a way to experience India's architectural history without the formality of museum visits or the logistics of fort tours. The venues combine cultural immersion with practical hospitality—a meal at Adaa or Baradari can anchor an afternoon in a way that a quick walk through a palace cannot.

Several of these restaurants have also become destination dining experiences in their own right, featured in international travel guides and recommended by luxury hospitality brands, making them increasingly visible to NRIs planning itineraries from abroad.

What to Watch

The heritage dining trend shows no signs of slowing. Livemint recently reported on additional conversions in Mumbai, Goa, Lucknow and Mysuru, suggesting the model is expanding to new cities and building types—from Indo-Portuguese bungalows to Art Deco mansions. As more hospitality groups recognize the commercial potential of adaptive reuse, the pipeline of heritage restaurant conversions is likely to grow, offering both preservation advocates and food enthusiasts new reasons to seek out India's architectural past.
